questions.question: What can increase fatigue while riding?

options.text: Riding in cool, windy, or rainy weather.
Starting a ride late in the day.

questions.correctAnswerText: Riding in cool, windy, or rainy weather.
questions.explanation: To avoid fatigue, dress for bad weather like wind and rain. Do not ride more than six hours per day. Take a break at least every two hours. Do not use artificial stimulants because you will feel very tired when they wear off.

questions.question: Studies show that nearly ______ of motorcycle riders killed in crashes had been drinking.
questions.correctAnswerText: 40 percent
questions.explanation: Alcohol is a major cause of motorcycle crashes and deaths. Research shows that about 40 percent of all motorcycle riders killed in accidents had been drinking.

questions.question: What should you do to reduce your reaction time?

options.text: Ride slower than the speed limit.
Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes.
Shift into neutral when slowing down.
Pull in the clutch when turning.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes.
questions.explanation: Keep your hands ready on the clutch and brakes to react faster. This is especially important when riding where hazards might appear.

questions.question: If a passing vehicle creates a wind blast that hits you, where should you be riding to have the most room to correct your motorcycle?

options.text: In the left part of the lane.
In the center of the lane.
In the right part of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the center of the lane.
questions.explanation: Riding in the center of your lane gives you the most space to recover if a wind blast pushes you.

questions.question: Proper riding clothes provide all of the following except:
questions.correctAnswerText: Discomfort.
questions.explanation: Proper clothing protects you from crashes and bad weather like heat and cold. It does not cause discomfort—it prevents it.

questions.question: Which statement is true about motorcycle brakes?

options.text: The front and rear brakes provide equal stopping power.
The front brake provides more stopping power than the rear brake.
The rear brake provides more stopping power than the front brake.
Use only the front brake when stopping.

questions.correctAnswerText: The front brake provides more stopping power than the rear brake.
questions.explanation: The front brake is more powerful and provides at least 70 percent of your stopping power. Always use both brakes when you slow down or stop.

questions.question: Where should less experienced riders position themselves in a group?

options.text: At the back of the group.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Less experienced riders should stay just behind the leader. This allows more experienced riders behind them to watch and help if needed.

questions.question: What should motorcycle riders do about hearing protection?

options.text: Always wear hearing protection to prevent hearing damage.
Only wear hearing protection on long rides.
Do not wear hearing protection because it blocks horns and sirens.
Skip hearing protection if you wear a helmet.

questions.correctAnswerText: Always wear hearing protection to prevent hearing damage.
questions.explanation: Wind and engine noise can cause permanent hearing loss over time, even with a helmet. Earplugs protect your hearing while still letting you hear horns and sirens.

questions.question: A rectangular sign could be a:
questions.correctAnswerText: Speed limit sign.
questions.explanation: Speed limit signs are rectangular with white backgrounds and black letters. They tell you the rules you must follow on the road.

questions.question: Which idea should you NOT use when planning a long group ride?

options.text: Plan travel distances based on the least experienced rider.
Skip breaks so everyone reaches the destination faster.
Place less experienced riders behind the leaders.

questions.correctAnswerText: Skip breaks so everyone reaches the destination faster.
questions.explanation: Plan distances based on the least experienced rider. Take regular breaks to reduce fatigue. Place less experienced riders behind experienced riders who can watch them. Ride in a staggered formation.

questions.question: Where should inexperienced riders be placed when riding in a group?

options.text: In the front of the group.
At the back of the group.

questions.correctAnswerText: Just behind the lead rider.
questions.explanation: Inexperienced riders should ride just behind the leader. This way, experienced riders can watch them from behind.

questions.question: When riding at night, which of the following should you NOT do?

options.text: Use the headlights of vehicles ahead to help you see.
Ride only in the left portion of your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride only in the left portion of your lane.
questions.explanation: At night, use your high beam, use other vehicles' headlights to see better, and wear reflective materials. Move around your lane to see better and stay safe. Don't stay only on the left side.

questions.question: What collects in the center portion of a traffic lane?

options.text: Debris and oil drippings from cars.
Motorcycle riders travel here for safety.
Drivers are least likely to see a motorcyclist.

questions.correctAnswerText: Debris and oil drippings from cars.
questions.explanation: The center of a lane collects debris and oil from cars. Manhole covers and other hazards are also found in this area.

questions.question: What should you do to reduce your reaction time?
questions.correctAnswerText: Cover the clutch and brakes.
questions.explanation: When approaching danger, like an intersection, hold your fingers on the clutch lever and both brakes. This makes you ready to react quickly.

questions.question: How do motorcycle headlights compare to car headlights?

options.text: Usually more powerful than a car's headlights.
Usually just as powerful as a car's headlights.
Usually not as powerful as a car's headlights.
Usually larger than a car's headlights.

questions.correctAnswerText: Usually not as powerful as a car's headlights.
questions.explanation: Motorcycle headlights are smaller and weaker than car headlights.

questions.question: How should you swerve correctly?

options.text: Press the handle grip in the direction you plan to swerve.
Press the handle grip in the direction opposite of where you plan to swerve.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handle grip in the direction you plan to swerve.
questions.explanation: To swerve left, press the left handle grip, then press the right to straighten. To swerve right, press the right handle grip, then the left. Use light pressure.

questions.question: Why should you not ride too far to the right of your lane on a three-wheeled motorcycle or with a sidecar?

options.text: Other drivers may not see you.
You will not be able to pass other vehicles as easily.
Other drivers may try to share your lane.
You may run off the road.

questions.correctAnswerText: You may run off the road.
questions.explanation: A sidecar sits on the right side. If you ride too far right, the sidecar may leave the road. On a three-wheeled motorcycle, the right rear wheel could also go off the road.

questions.question: Which factor does NOT affect a person's blood alcohol content (BAC)?

options.text: How quickly the alcohol was consumed

questions.correctAnswerText: How often alcohol is consumed
questions.explanation: Three main things affect BAC: the amount of alcohol consumed, how quickly it was consumed, and body weight. Sex, fitness level, and food intake also matter. How often someone drinks does not affect their BAC.

questions.question: What guarantees that another driver sees you?
questions.correctAnswerText: Nothing
questions.explanation: Nothing guarantees that a driver sees you. Always assume that if another vehicle could enter your path, it will.

questions.question: Which formation should a group of riders use when entering a curve?
questions.correctAnswerText: Single-file
questions.explanation: Use a staggered formation when riding in a group to maintain distance and safe spacing. Use single-file when taking curves, turning, or entering or exiting a highway.

questions.question: What color is a warning sign?

options.text: Yellow with black lettering or symbols

questions.correctAnswerText: Yellow with black lettering or symbols
questions.explanation: Warning signs are yellow with black lettering or symbols. They alert drivers to upcoming road conditions and hazards.

questions.question: Your lane position should do all of the following, except:

options.text: Help you see and be seen by others.
Keep you out of other drivers' blind spots.
Discourage other drivers from sharing your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Reduce your escape routes.
questions.explanation: Good lane position helps you see others and be seen. It keeps you out of blind spots, protects your lane, and gives you escape routes if a hazard appears. You should never position yourself to limit your escape routes.

questions.question: When riding in groups, can motorcyclists ride two abreast?

options.text: No, riders are never allowed to ride two abreast.
Yes, if both riders agree to it.
Only on roads with more than three lanes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Yes, if both riders agree to it.
questions.explanation: Nevada law allows two motorcycles to ride side-by-side in the same lane if both riders consent. A staggered formation is safer, but riding two abreast with permission is legal.

questions.question: When riding a three-wheeled motorcycle through a curve, what should you do?

options.text: Stay in the center of the lane.
Stay on the outside of the lane.
Adjust your path as the curve requires.

questions.correctAnswerText: Adjust your path as the curve requires.
questions.explanation: Three-wheeled motorcycles handle differently than two-wheeled ones. You may need to move from the outside of the curve to the inside before straightening out. Follow the path that works best for your three-wheeler, not the curve itself.

questions.question: If you cannot avoid hitting an object in the road, what should you do?
questions.correctAnswerText: Slow down before hitting it.
questions.explanation: Slow down as much as you can before impact. Keep your motorcycle upright, rise slightly off the seat, and ease off the throttle to lighten the front wheel just before you hit the object.
